query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing minor amounts of Ge and B into a refractory high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, protective SiO2 scale during high-temperature oxygen exposure, thereby improving its oxygen resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) without Ge and B additions, containing sufficient silicon to form SiO2 but typically forming discontinuous oxide scales under high-temperature exposure.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding minor quantities of Ge (e.g., around 6 at.%) and B.
generation.conditions: Exposure at high temperatures between 700 °C and 900 °C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (e.g., air with PO2 ≈ 0.21 atm) for extended periods (e.g., on the order of 100 hours) to simulate extreme-temperature service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous and dense SiO2 scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Ge is expected to destabilize competing silicide phases and enhance oxide adhesion, while B acts as a glass network former, improving the sealing and densification of the SiO2 layer. This synergistic action promotes a continuous protective oxide scale that limits oxygen diffusion into the underlying alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will show a markedly reduced oxidation rate, improved integrity of the protective scale, and overall enhanced high-temperature oxygen resistance compared with the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated refractory HEA typically exhibits discontinuous or less protective oxide scales, leading to higher oxidation rates and degradation under similar exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected primarily for HEAs that are silicon-rich enough to form SiO2 and under temperatures between 700 °C and 900 °C in atmospheric oxygen; deviations outside these parameters may not yield the same benefit.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum concentrations of Ge and B and the exact quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance require further experimental validation. Additionally, the alloy’s specific composition and processing history may influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one using the standard refractory HEA composition and one with the modified composition including Ge and B. Expose both sets to air at 850 °C for 100 hours. After exposure, analyze the surface using SEM for scale morphology, XRD for phase identification, and weight gain measurements for oxidation rate.
measurements: Continuity and phase composition of the oxide scale (via SEM, TEM, and XRD)
Adhesion tests of the oxide scale
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ge and B–modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant lower oxidation weight gain and improved oxide scale continuity/adhesion compared to the untreated alloy under the tested conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of Ge and B improved the protective SiO2 phase grown during high-temperature oxidation and resulted in the formation of a continuous and dense oxide scale []. The addition of 6 at.% Ge in Nb-22Ti-12Si destabilised the Nb3Si, promoted the formation of Nb5Si3, significantly refined the microstructure and improved the high-temperature strength and room temperature fracture toughness respectively by about 88 and 19%, compared with the alloy without Ge []. The fracture toughness (KC, 3–point bend) of as-cast and heat-treated Nb-Ti-Si-Cr-Hf-Ge solid solution and silicide based alloys and the indentation toughness of the solid solution, Laves, and silicide phases have been reported []. The fracture toughness was not significantly changed by heat treatment and was about 10 MPa·m1/2 for alloys with more than 50 vol % silicide and Laves phases while the toughness of the solid solution ranged from 22 to 32 MPa·m1/2.

reading.lever: Introduce minor Ge and B into the refractory HEA to promote in-situ formation of a continuous, protective SiO₂ scale during high-temperature exposure.
reading.why: Prior evidence shows Ge and B additions significantly improve oxide scale integrity in Nb-Ti-Si alloys, suggesting similar benefits for refractory HEAs under extreme-temperature conditions.
